summary.headline: Profits are recovering, but they swing with aluminium prices and debt has climbed to nearly twice equity
summary.text: Alumex PLC (ALUM.N0000), Sri Lanka's largest aluminium extrusion maker and a Hayleys subsidiary (52.6%), is earning more: profit for the six months to September 2026 was Rs 268mn against Rs 69mn, and the September quarter's operating profit rose 75%. But at Rs 17.60 the share trades at 2.0x its NAV of Rs 8.98, and its trailing P/E of 9.9x rests on one exceptional quarter (January–March 2026, EPS Rs 1.40, lifted by rising aluminium prices and fire insurance). Profit swings with aluminium prices (a loss in 2022/23, almost nothing in 2023/24), and net debt has risen to Rs 10.0bn, 1.9x equity, as stock was built up against Middle East supply problems. That debt also makes the share risky, so the required return is high (23.7%). On normal earnings the methods put fair value at about Rs 4.20, a quarter of the price. I'd buy only at up to about Rs 3.60 and treat under Rs 3.20 as a strong buy: in practice, not a share to buy at today's price.

highlights.title: Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited)
highlights.text: Revenue rose 13% to Rs 8.60bn, gross margin improved to 20.5% from 16.1%, and operating profit rose 51% to Rs 727mn. Profit was Rs 268mn (EPS Rs 0.45) against Rs 69mn. The September quarter alone: revenue +28%, operating profit +75%, but finance costs +56%, so profit was Rs 118mn (EPS Rs 0.20).

highlights.title: Stock and debt up sharply
highlights.text: Inventory rose from Rs 4.43bn to Rs 7.25bn in six months (management is holding bigger buffers against billet supply problems), paid for with short-term loans: borrowings Rs 10.1bn, net debt Rs 10.0bn (1.9x equity). Operating cash flow was −Rs 2.07bn.

highlights.title: 2025/26: one big quarter
highlights.text: Revenue Rs 16.94bn (+18%), profit Rs 863mn (flat), EPS Rs 1.44. January–March 2026 earned Rs 1.40 of it, helped by rising LME aluminium prices and Rs 211mn of business-interruption insurance from the 2024/25 Ekala fire. Operating profit without insurance rose 25% to Rs 1.59bn.

highlights.title: Exports shifting away from the US
highlights.text: US tariffs of 50% cut exports there by 28%, while Europe (+56%) and Australia (+47%) grew; exports were 35% of revenue. Only 39% of the 24,000 MT extrusion capacity was used.

highlights.title: Interim dividend
highlights.text: Rs 0.20 a share declared for 2026/27 (none at this point last year); Rs 0.47 was paid for 2025/26.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: NAV Rs 8.98 × (long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): ROE 11% / 15% / 19%, growth 4% / 5% / 6%, cost of equity 25.2% / 23.7% / 22.2%. Even the bull ROE is below the required return, so value is below book.

models.name: P/E method (justified P/E)
models.comment: EPS for the year to March 2027 of Rs 0.85 / 1.20 / 1.55 × justified P/E of 3.0 / 3.6 / 4.2 (from ROE, growth and the cost of equity). Base EPS is 32% below the Rs 1.77 run-rate because that includes the March 2026 quarter's metal-price gains and Rs 211mn of one-off insurance; H1 EPS is Rs 0.45 and the base case assumes Rs 0.75 in the second half.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book Rs 8.98, ROE moving from 15% to 11% / 15% / 19% over 10 years, 33% payout, then growth 4% / 5% / 6%, at a 25.2% / 23.7% / 22.2% cost of equity.

modelsNote: Three methods are weighted: justified price to book, P/E and residual income. A whole-company DCF was run (scripts/reinvestment.py): start cash Rs 0.52 / 0.96 / 1.40bn (2025/26 operating cash plus after-tax interest, less maintenance capex of Rs 1.32 / 0.88 / 0.43bn), growth 3% / 6% / 8% for five years then 4% / 5% / 6%, return on new capital 9% / 11% / 13%, at WACC 16.5% / 15.8% / 15.0%. Firm values of Rs 0.4 / 3.2 / 8.4bn are all below net debt of Rs 10.0bn, giving Rs −16.1 / −11.4 / −2.7 a share (71–75% of the base and bull value comes after year 5). It isn't weighted because operating cash swings by billions with stock levels (−Rs 1.37bn in 2023/24, +Rs 1.20bn in 2025/26, −Rs 2.07bn in the half to September), but it is a warning: on its record the business hasn't produced enough cash to support its debt. A dividend model isn't weighted either: the payout is a third of profit, so it would understate value. Growth check: assumed 3% / 6% / 8% against 5.6% supported (49% of after-tax operating profit reinvested × 11.3% return on capital); the bull case is 2.4 points above because only 39% of extrusion capacity is used, so volumes can grow without new plant.

scenarios.common: NAV Rs 8.98 and net debt Rs 10.01bn at 30 September 2026; 598.6 million shares. Payout 33%. Residual income starts at 15% ROE. Price Rs 17.60 (CSE close, 19 November 2026).

sensitivity.title: Residual income base case, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: The required return matters most. At the 17% used in the first analysis the three methods would give a fair value of about Rs 7.10; at 20%, about Rs 5.50. Even then, today's Rs 17.60 needs ROE well above 20% for many years.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 1,860 in total, against Rs 8,800 at Rs 17.60.
buyPlan.realism: Rs 4.23 needs a fall of about 76%. The lowest year-end price in ten years was Rs 7.20 (March 2020) and the low since April 2024 is Rs 9.50, so the buy price isn't realistic. This is a share to avoid at today's price rather than to wait for.

higher: Profit holding near Rs 1.5–2 a share without insurance or metal-price gains.
Stock sold down and short-term loans repaid, bringing net debt below equity (that would also lower the beta and the required return).
Exports to Europe, Australia and India (now open after BIS certification) filling the idle 61% of extrusion capacity.
The EBIT margin reaching the 20% target.
lower: Aluminium prices falling, so stock bought at high prices loses value.
Construction slowing, or BOI projects importing finished doors and windows again.
Interest rates rising on Rs 8.8bn of short-term loans.
Billet supply from the Middle East staying disrupted, raising costs.
A return to the losses of 2022/23.

fullText:
Summary: Alumex PLC (ALUM.N0000), Sri Lanka's largest aluminium extrusion maker and a Hayleys subsidiary (52.6%), is earning more: profit for the six months to September 2026 was Rs 268mn against Rs 69mn, and the September quarter's operating profit rose 75%. But at Rs 17.60 the share trades at 2.0x its NAV of Rs 8.98, and its trailing P/E of 9.9x rests on one exceptional quarter (January–March 2026, EPS Rs 1.40, lifted by rising aluminium prices and fire insurance). Profit swings with aluminium prices (a loss in 2022/23, almost nothing in 2023/24), and net debt has risen to Rs 10.0bn, 1.9x equity, as stock was built up against Middle East supply problems. That debt also makes the share risky, so the required return is high (23.7%). On normal earnings the methods put fair value at about Rs 4.20, a quarter of the price. I'd buy only at up to about Rs 3.60 and treat under Rs 3.20 as a strong buy: in practice, not a share to buy at today's price.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 17.60 (CSE close, 19 November 2026). It traded at Rs 16.00–19.90 in April–June 2026 and Rs 15.70–17.90 in July–September 2026; Rs 13.50–22.70 in the year to March 2026.
Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 8.60bn (+13%), gross margin 20.5% (16.1%), operating profit Rs 727mn (+51%), profit Rs 268mn (Rs 69mn), EPS Rs 0.45 (Rs 0.12). The September quarter: revenue Rs 5.02bn (+28%), operating profit Rs 456mn (+75%), finance costs Rs 331mn (+56%), profit Rs 118mn, EPS Rs 0.20. Interim dividend Rs 0.20.
Balance sheet at September 2026: inventory Rs 7.25bn (Rs 4.43bn in March), borrowings Rs 10.10bn (short-term Rs 8.85bn), leases Rs 0.37bn, cash Rs 0.46bn, so net debt Rs 10.01bn, 1.86x equity of Rs 5.38bn. Operating cash flow for the half was −Rs 2.07bn.
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 16.94bn (+18%; exports 35%), operating profit Rs 1.77bn (Rs 1.59bn without Rs 184mn net insurance income), profit Rs 863mn (Rs 867mn), EPS Rs 1.44, ROE 17%, dividend Rs 0.47. January–March 2026 earned EPS Rs 1.40, helped by rising LME aluminium prices and Rs 211mn of business-interruption insurance from the 2024/25 Ekala fire. Operating cash flow Rs 1.20bn, mostly from selling down stock; capex Rs 909mn. Only 39% of the 24,000 MT extrusion capacity was used.
Cycle: EPS from 2016/17 to 2025/26 was Rs 1.26, 0.61, 0.21, 0.05, 1.40, 1.92, −0.02, 0.31, 1.45 and 1.44. ROE averaged about 16.6%. Operating cash over the last five years totalled −Rs 0.43bn against Rs 3.06bn of profit.

Required return
Beta 1.50 (provisional): Damodaran's global Building Materials unlevered beta of 0.90, relevered for net debt of 0.95x market value. Cost of equity 8.24% + 1.50 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = 23.7% (bear 25.2%, bull 22.2%). That's above the usual 12–22% for CSE shares because the company's borrowings are nearly as large as its market value. Cost of debt 8.9%; WACC 15.8%.

Methods
NAV (Rs 8.98): the price is 2.0x.
Return on equity: 17% in 2025/26, below the 23.7% required return.
P/E: 9.9x trailing EPS of Rs 1.77, which includes the exceptional March 2026 quarter.
Justified price to book: Rs 2.97 / 4.80 / 7.21, weighted Rs 4.73.
P/E method (justified P/E): Rs 2.55 / 4.28 / 6.55, weighted Rs 4.21.
Residual income: Rs 2.54 / 3.74 / 5.65, weighted Rs 3.76.
Whole-company DCF (not weighted): firm value Rs 0.4 / 3.2 / 8.4bn, all below net debt of Rs 10.0bn, so below zero a share. Cash flow swings too much with stock to rely on, but it shows that the business hasn't produced enough cash to carry its debt.
Dividend model: not weighted; the payout is a third of profit.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity 25.2% / 23.7% / 22.2%. Long-run ROE 11% / 15% / 19%. Long-term growth 4% / 5% / 6%. EPS for the year to March 2027 Rs 0.85 / 1.20 / 1.55 (H1 Rs 0.45; base second half Rs 0.75, well below last year's Rs 1.32, which had insurance and metal-price gains), times a justified P/E of 3.0 / 3.6 / 4.2. Growth for five years 3% / 6% / 8% against 5.6% supported by reinvestment; the bull case can run above it because 61% of extrusion capacity is idle.
Averages of the three methods: Rs 2.69 / 4.27 / 6.47.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value (30/50/20): Rs 4.23, about 0.47x NAV. The price is about four times that.
Buy price (15% margin): Rs 3.60. Strong buy (25%): Rs 3.17.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 4.23, 150 at up to Rs 3.60, 150 at up to Rs 3.17: average about Rs 3.72, about Rs 1,860, against Rs 8,800 at Rs 17.60.
Realism: a fall of about 76% is needed; the share's lowest year-end price in ten years was Rs 7.20 (2020). Not realistic: avoid at today's price.

Why the value fell from Rs 8.40 (9 November 2026)
Two reasons. The required return is now worked out from the beta (23.7%, against 17% chosen by hand before), and the P/E method now uses the P/E that the cost of equity, ROE and growth justify (3.0–4.2x) instead of the 7–11x used before. At a 17% cost of equity the methods would still give only about Rs 7.10.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share; long-run ROE 11% / 15% / 19%)
Cost of equity 17%: 4.59 / 6.99 / 9.93. 20%: 3.51 / 5.11 / 7.05. 23.7%: 2.70 / 3.74 / 4.98.

Management and plans
Management plans to cut stock to 130 days, lift the EBIT margin to 20% within two years and 22% later, and swap short-term loans for long-term ones. So far stock, short-term loans and gearing have all gone up, as the company built buffers against Middle East billet supply problems. The Rs 740mn modernisation (new extrusion line, second die-casting plant) was completed. EPS slipped slightly in 2025/26, missing the promise to raise it every year.

Shareholders
Hayleys PLC holds 52.59%; the MD 3.56%. Public holding 39.00% (8,630 holders). The top 20 was unchanged in the September quarter apart from 20th place.

What would change my view
Higher: profit holding near Rs 1.5–2 a share without one-offs; stock and short-term loans coming down (net debt below equity would also lower the required return); exports filling idle capacity; the EBIT margin reaching 20%.
Lower: aluminium prices falling; construction slowing; higher interest rates on Rs 8.8bn of short-term loans; billet supply problems; a return to losses.

These are my estimates from the annual report to March 2026 and the interim reports to June and September 2026. The September interim is a scanned image, read from the page images; check any figure that matters. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
